sector: Healthcare Services (NZ Primary Care / Aged Residential Care Medical Services)
overview: Third Age Health Services Limited is New Zealand's leading dedicated provider of managed primary medical services to the aged residential care (ARC) sector, delivering GP and Nurse Practitioner-led care to residents in rest homes, private hospitals, secure dementia units and retirement villages nationwide, alongside a smaller general practice business serving the wider community in Auckland and Hawke's Bay. Now 15+ years old, TAH operates as a national platform built through organic facility wins and disciplined bolt-on acquisitions of founder-owned ARC medical practices. Revenue is funded predominantly through NZ Government primary care capitation (via PHOs) and fee-for-service consultations, and the company operates exclusively within New Zealand. From H1 FY27, ARC Medical Services and Community GP have been formally decentralised into two distinct operating businesses, each with its own general manager.

business_model.summary: TAH generates revenue through two segments: ARC Medical Services (H1 FY27 revenue $9.153M, +33.9% YoY, ~71% of group revenue) and Community General Practice ($3.714M, -2.6% YoY, ~29% of group revenue). Revenue is largely recurring — monthly capitation payments from PHOs based on enrolled-patient counts and demographics, supplemented by per-visit consultation fees. The model is asset-light (clinicians deliver care within client-owned ARC facilities or leased GP clinic premises under service contracts), giving high operating leverage as the patient base scales. TAH grows the ARC segment through bolt-on acquisition of small, founder-owned ARC medical practices at modest multiples, integrated using its 'Third Age Way of Working' (TAWoW) Kaizen-based operating system, and has stopped acquiring further Community GP practices after negative experience with small-practice economics (Belmont Medical Centre closure, formally exited with lease derecognition in October 2026). H1 FY27 group results: revenue $12.867M (+20.8% YoY), EBITDA $3.700M (+34.1% YoY), statutory NPAT $2.104M (+38.4% YoY), of which $1.841M attributable to shareholders of the parent (+30.2% YoY) and $263k to non-controlling interests; diluted EPS 18.50 cents (+30.1% YoY). Of H1 FY27 revenue, $1.568M came from businesses acquired within the prior 12 months (ARC Health and Cicada Health, which completed their first 12 months of ownership on 31 August 2026 and transition to 'existing operations' from September 2026), with the remaining $11.299M from existing operations.

revenue_streams.name: Community General Practice (capitation + consultation)
revenue_streams.trend: stable/low-growth, patient attrition largely offset by pricing

business_model.customer_type: B2B (ARC facility operators as primary clients; NZ Government / Health NZ / PHOs as primary funder; individual ARC residents and GP patients as end-users)
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand. National ARC footprint including Auckland, Wellington/Lower North Island, Northland, Canterbury (via ARC Health, Sept 2025) and Bay of Plenty (via Cicada Health, Sept 2025), spanning 124+ ARC facilities as of the last disclosed count (Q1 FY27, July 2026). Community GP concentrated in Auckland (Devonport, Ponsonby) and Hawke's Bay. No foreign operations or currency exposure.

main_competitors: Independent/owner-operator GPs and small regional GP networks servicing ARC facilities on an ad hoc basis
Large integrated aged-care operators (Ryman Healthcare, Bupa NZ, Summerset, Oceania Healthcare, Metlifecare, Arvida) — indirect competition where facilities manage medical services in-house
Locum GP/NP staffing agencies (compete for scarce clinician supply rather than for facility contracts)
General practice owner-operators and PHOs more broadly, for Community GP patient enrolments
competitive_position.market_position: Largest dedicated national provider of managed primary medical care to ARC facilities in New Zealand, with an estimated ~17-18% share of the ARC medical services market and a stated medium-term target of 20%. No competitor operates at equivalent national scale in this specific niche. Named sole preferred medical services partner by the Aged Care Association New Zealand (Sept 2025). ARC segment revenue growth accelerated to +33.9% YoY in H1 FY27 (from +27% in FY26), reflecting both the full-period contribution of the ARC Health/Cicada Health acquisitions and continued organic momentum.

moat_factors.description: National footprint across 124+ ARC facilities (as of the last disclosed count), expanded into Canterbury and Bay of Plenty via the FY26 ARC Health and Cicada Health acquisitions, gives TAH a clinician network, rostering infrastructure, and management system that small-scale competitors cannot easily replicate. Facility relationships tend to be sticky given the operational burden of switching medical service providers.

Digital Clinical Portal live in 30+ facilities (from 13 at March 2025), supporting 900+ scheduled clinical rounds. Paired with TAH's independently-audited 'Residential Care Medical Service Provider Standard' (Elder Care Standards), this creates differentiation versus the fragmented visiting-clinician norm. The H1 FY27 Chairman's letter signals a step-up in technology and cybersecurity investment going forward, 'accepting some cost to short-term earnings in return for greater durability over time' — a deliberate widening of this moat even at a near-term margin cost.

moat_factors.factor: PHO contract relationships and regulatory/administrative complexity
moat_factors.description: Capitation revenue flows via PHO agreements recognised as intangible assets on acquisition ($3.206M of non-goodwill intangibles at 30 September 2026). Navigating ARC-specific enrolment rules and maintaining PHO relationships is a meaningful barrier for new entrants. Sole preferred partner status with the Aged Care Association New Zealand reinforces sector standing.

NP Development Programme and structured GP training pathways provide a partially self-sustaining talent funnel in an otherwise severely undersupplied labour market — a structural differentiator smaller operators cannot fund.

moat_factors.factor: Kaizen / TAWoW operating model and decentralised management
moat_factors.description: The 'Third Age Way of Working' provides a standardised, low-cost playbook for onboarding new facilities and integrating acquisitions. From H1 FY27, the Chairman's letter describes a deliberate decentralisation: ARC Medical Services and Community GP now run as distinct businesses under dedicated GMs (Crystal Murphy and Greg Clarke respectively), with the Group centre focused on TAWoW support and capital allocation. Management also flagged that rapid growth had allowed 'more complexity than was necessary' in systems and processes, and is now actively simplifying — a candid acknowledgement that execution quality needs active maintenance as the platform scales.

weaknesses: Small absolute scale (H1 FY27 revenue run-rate ~NZ$26M annualised; market cap roughly NZ$46-48M at a recent share price near NZ$4.6-4.8) limits negotiating leverage with Health NZ/PHOs and constrains access to low-cost capital

Community GP segment (~29% of H1 FY27 revenue) revenue declined 2.6% YoY and segment profit before tax fell sharply to $258k from $494k in the prior comparable half (segment EBITDA $735k vs $978k), even as the ARC segment's profitability surged — the GP business remains a drag on group margin and growth
Dependent on an acutely thin clinician labour market — ARC growth has been described by management as constrained by clinical workforce availability, not by demand

Management explicitly flagged accumulated operational complexity from rapid multi-entity growth (different systems, processes and ways of working across acquired practices) requiring active simplification work in H1 FY27 and beyond

Minority-owned subsidiaries (Hub Aged Care 70%, ARC Health 80%, Cicada Health 70%, EastMed 67%) create governance complexity and NCI dilution of parent earnings — NCI's share of H1 FY27 group profit rose to $263k (12.5% of total) from $105k (6.9%) in the prior comparable half, growing faster than the group as a whole

NZX micro-cap illiquidity; share price has historically swung across a wide range (the Chairman previously cited a ~3x range of NZ$2.50-$7.50 during FY26); zero sell-side analyst coverage was found (TipRanks/Simply Wall St/Stockopedia all show 0 covering analysts), reinforcing thin, potentially inefficient price discovery

Belmont Medical Centre practice (previously closed after safety incidents) had its lease formally vacated and derecognised only in October 2026 (a post-period subsequent event in the H1 FY27 accounts), roughly 15 months after the underlying closure — illustrating a slow final unwind of a failed small-practice acquisition

growth_drivers: NZ demographic tailwind: population aged 65+ was ~16.6% of NZ in 2023 (up from 12.3% in 2006) and is projected to reach ~28% by 2073; the 65+ dependency ratio is projected to rise from ~25 per 100 working-age people (2024) to 43-57 per 100 by 2078. This is a multi-decade, non-cyclical structural demand driver for ARC medical services.

ARC market share expansion: TAH targets ~20% of the ARC medical services market (from an estimated ~17-18%), via organic facility wins and further bolt-on acquisitions. ARC segment revenue grew 33.9% YoY in H1 FY27 to $9.153M, with segment profit before tax more than 63% higher YoY ($2.696M vs $1.651M) and segment EBITDA up 66% YoY ($2.965M vs $1.781M) — the clearest evidence yet that the acquired ARC Health/Cicada Health businesses plus organic growth are driving genuine operating leverage, not just revenue growth.

Bolt-on acquisitions at attractive multiples, ARC-focused: Hub Aged Care (April 2024), ARC Health and Cicada Health (Sept 2025) were all immediately EBITDA-accretive with founders remaining as active co-owners. The deferred contingent consideration for ARC Health and Cicada Health ($498,750 combined) was paid in full during H1 FY27, cleanly closing out that acquisition's balance-sheet tail. No new acquisition has been announced since September 2025 (over 14 months), though management's capital-allocation language in the H1 FY27 letter continues to point toward prudent ongoing M&A.

ARC capitation rate increases and reweighting now in effect: the demographically-reweighted capitation formula (age, sex, multimorbidity, rurality, socioeconomic deprivation) took effect 1 July 2026 after an 86% GP-practice vote in favour of Health NZ's 2026-27 funding package (6.32% base increase, guaranteed minimum 4% per-practice increase, $128.4M additional government investment). H1 FY27's ARC capitation revenue grew to $2.940M from $1.875M YoY (+57%), well ahead of ARC consultation revenue growth (+25% YoY), consistent with the reweighted formula benefiting TAH's older, higher-acuity ARC population, though the acquisition-driven facility growth also contributes to this and the two effects are not separately disclosed.

Digital Clinical Portal rollout: live in 30+ facilities (from 13 at March 2025), supporting 900+ scheduled clinical rounds, with further phases planned. Reduces per-patient administrative cost, improves care quality metrics, and strengthens client retention.

Decentralised operating model: formal separation of ARC Medical Services (under Crystal Murphy) and Community GP (under Greg Clarke) into distinct businesses from H1 FY27, intended to sharpen accountability and decision speed closer to the customer — if executed well, this should let the higher-growth ARC business scale without being slowed by the Group center managing two very different businesses with one playbook.

AI and virtual care: AI transcription tools reducing clinician documentation burden; telehealth/virtual care solutions extending after-hours ARC coverage, effectively expanding clinician capacity without proportional headcount growth.

Technology/cybersecurity investment step-up: management flagged in the H1 FY27 letter a deliberate increase in investment in cybersecurity and technology infrastructure, 'accepting some cost to short-term earnings in return for greater durability over time' — a long-term moat and risk-mitigation investment following the sector-wide Manage My Health breach.

business.description: The large majority of TAH's revenue ultimately flows from Health New Zealand (Te Whatu Ora), either as capitation via PHOs or consultation fee schedules. The FY27 capitation package (6.32% base uplift, reweighted formula, effective 1 July 2026) was agreed and implemented and is now flowing through H1 FY27 results, removing near-term funding-freeze risk, but TAH remains structurally a price-taker in the government-funded primary care system. Cabinet has agreed to review capitation every five years (first review from 2028), which sets the next point of funding-policy uncertainty.

business.risk: Clinical workforce shortage and wage inflation
business.description: NZ faces a structural GP/NP shortage (over half of GPs aged 50+, a meaningful share of practices closed to new enrolments, a multi-year projected GP deficit). ARC growth has been described by management as capacity-constrained by clinician availability. Practitioner costs (GPs and nurses) rose to $6.108M in H1 FY27 from $5.127M in the prior comparable half (+19.1%), broadly tracking revenue growth; total cost of services rose to $6.300M (48.9% of revenue) from $5.258M (49.4% of revenue), a modest gross-margin improvement, but clinician remuneration remains the dominant and least-controllable cost line.

business.risk: Community GP segment profitability decline and small-practice fragility
business.description: Community GP segment revenue fell 2.6% YoY in H1 FY27 ($3.714M vs $3.813M) and segment profit before tax fell to $258k from $494k YoY, with segment EBITDA down to $735k from $978k — a meaningfully worse outcome than the modest revenue decline alone suggests, implying cost growth or mix pressure within the GP business even under new dedicated leadership (Greg Clarke). The Belmont Medical Centre site, closed after safety incidents, only had its lease formally vacated and derecognised in October 2026 — a reminder of the slow, costly tail of exiting a failed small-practice acquisition.

business.risk: Leadership transition and decentralisation execution risk
business.description: ARC Medical Services and Community GP were formally split into distinct businesses from H1 FY27 under new GMs Crystal Murphy (ARC) and Greg Clarke (GP) — both appear to be new appointments following Niomi Fleming's July 2026 departure from the ARC GM role and Lucy Wu's prior acting role in Community GP; neither new GM's track record at TAH is yet established through a full reporting cycle. The Chairman's letter itself flags that rapid growth left the business more operationally complex than intended, which the new structure and 'simplify and consolidate systems' initiative are meant to address — successful execution of both the leadership handover and the simplification programme is not yet proven.

DOWNGRADED from moderate: the deferred contingent consideration for ARC Health ($280k) and Cicada Health ($218.75k), totalling $498,750, was paid in full during H1 FY27, cleanly resolving the prior period's open item with no disclosed dispute or clawback. Minority co-ownership of four subsidiaries (Hub Aged Care 70%, ARC Health 80%, Cicada Health 70%, EastMed 67%) continues to add governance complexity and a growing NCI claim on consolidated earnings (12.5% of H1 FY27 profit, up from 6.9% YoY), but no new acquisition-related risk has emerged.

TAH issued a patient communications update in January 2026 relating to the Manage My Health (MMH) cybersecurity breach in late 2025 (MMH is a third-party patient portal used across NZ primary care); no material financial impact has been disclosed. Management's H1 FY27 letter signals an ongoing, deliberate increase in cybersecurity and technology-infrastructure investment ('accepting some cost to short-term earnings'), indicating this remains an active area of focus and residual risk rather than a closed issue.

financial.risk: Small-cap illiquidity and volatile market pricing
financial.description: With roughly 9.95M shares outstanding and a market cap in the roughly NZ$46-48M range at a recent price near NZ$4.6-4.8, TAH is a micro-cap with thin trading volumes and zero sell-side analyst coverage identified (TipRanks, Simply Wall St and Stockopedia each show 0 covering analysts). The Chairman previously disclosed a ~3x intra-year trading range (NZ$2.50-$7.50) during FY26, which he described as an unrealistic assessment of intrinsic value at both ends. This limits institutional participation, widens bid-ask spreads, and constrains TAH's ability to use equity as acquisition currency.

financial.risk: Bank debt and lease liabilities at floating/contracted rates
financial.description: As at 30 September 2026, TAH carried $1.061M in bank loans (current + non-current) and $2.346M in lease liabilities; the company confirmed compliance with all banking covenants for the period. Total debt remains modest relative to annualised EBITDA (H1 FY27 EBITDA of $3.700M). Interest rate risk is limited but real; finance costs rose to $162k in H1 FY27 from $138k YoY, including $34k of interest on deferred consideration (now settled) and modestly higher lease/bank-loan interest.

financial.risk: Intangible asset base and amortisation growth
financial.description: Intangible assets (goodwill $3.143M plus other intangibles $3.206M) totalled $6.349M at 30 September 2026, little changed from $6.673M at 31 March 2026 as no new acquisitions were made in the half. Amortisation and depreciation rose to $584k in H1 FY27 from $476k YoY (+22.7%), structurally reducing statutory NPAT relative to underlying cash generation as the acquisition portfolio is amortised. Management confirmed no Cash Generating Units showed indications of impairment as at 30 September 2026.

regulatory.risk: Health NZ funding reform and capitation reweighting
regulatory.description: The new capitation formula (incorporating age, sex, multimorbidity, rurality, and socioeconomic deprivation) took effect from 1 July 2026 and is now flowing through reported results (H1 FY27 ARC capitation revenue +57% YoY). Residual risk centres on the first scheduled five-yearly review of the formula from 2028, and on whether the current benefit to TAH's ARC-heavy patient mix persists through future funding cycles.

A government-convened advisory process on aged-care funding models has reportedly been underway, with potential implementation from 2027. Any shift toward bundled ARC-operator payments rather than direct GP capitation could fundamentally alter TAH's revenue model, though the stated government policy intent (reducing hospital pressure via stronger community/ARC care) is broadly supportive of TAH's role. No material update was identified in this review.

Ongoing Health NZ structural reform has reduced the number of PHOs nationally. If TAH's PHO partners merge or consolidate, contract renegotiation could affect capitation rates or enrolment terms. No specific adverse developments were identified in the review period.

macro.description: Health New Zealand agreed and funded a 2026-27 primary care package (6.32% base capitation uplift plus $128.4M additional investment), suggesting fiscal capacity to support primary care funding has not deteriorated further in the near term. TAH's revenue per enrolled patient nonetheless remains entirely dependent on future government funding decisions; any subsequent capitation freeze or reduction would directly compress margins given TAH's limited pricing power.

macro.risk: NZ economic conditions affecting GP co-payments
macro.description: TAH's ARC business is largely insulated from the economic cycle (ARC residents are government-funded). The Community GP segment earns some fee-for-service co-payments that could soften in a downturn, but this is a modest and shrinking share of total revenue (29% of H1 FY27 group revenue, down from 34% in FY26).

execution.description: Community GP segment profit before tax nearly halved YoY in H1 FY27 ($258k vs $494k) despite only a modest revenue decline, and the business now sits under a newly dedicated GM (Greg Clarke) following the decentralisation. Whether the new structure arrests the segment's multi-year profitability erosion, or whether further site rationalisation (as with Belmont) is required, will only become clear over the next 1-2 reporting periods.

execution.risk: Operational complexity from rapid multi-entity growth
execution.description: Management's own H1 FY27 letter acknowledges that growth and acquisition led to an accumulation of different systems, processes and ways of working, with 'more complexity than was necessary' in some areas, and describes an active simplification and consolidation programme. This is a candid, credible disclosure, but execution risk persists until the stated simplification is demonstrably completed.

In FY26 management evaluated (via term sheets that ultimately did not proceed) acquisitions outside healthcare in life-safety, compliance, and maintenance/repair/operations sectors. No new non-healthcare deal has been identified as completed or pending. Continued pursuit of adjacent-sector M&A introduces execution risk if management ventures into unfamiliar industries, even though discipline shown to date (walking away from term sheets that didn't meet return criteria) is a positive signal.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ aged-care demand is structurally growing on demographics: the 65+ share of population rose from 12.3% (2006) to 16.6% (2023) and is projected to reach ~28% by 2073, with the 65+ dependency ratio roughly doubling by 2078. ARC facility supply is constrained by land, construction costs and staffing, keeping occupancy high and demand for in-facility medical services growing in parallel. The primary care sector faces chronic structural underfunding (capitation formula unchanged since 2002 until now) but received its largest uplift in over a decade for FY26/FY27, with the demographically-reweighted formula now implemented and flowing through results from 1 July 2026 (86% GP-practice support, 6.32% base increase, $128.4M additional investment). GP/NP supply remains structurally short and is not expected to improve materially for 5-10 years. Management stated in the H1 FY27 interim report that 'the Group's current operations do not follow a seasonal or cyclical pattern.'
macro_factors.cyclicality: Very low. ARC medical services are non-discretionary healthcare funded primarily by government capitation; Community GP services are partially fee-based (co-payments) but still predominantly government-funded. TAH's revenue has grown through COVID-19 and NZ's 2023-24 economic slowdown without interruption, and growth accelerated further through H1 FY27.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct sensitivity — total debt (bank loans + leases) of roughly $3.4M at 30 September 2026 relative to H1 FY27 EBITDA of $3.700M (annualising to a very low leverage multiple). Indirect benefit from a declining NZ OCR (down from a 5.5% 2023-24 peak) reduces borrowing costs and supports continued acquisition financing.
macro_factors.currency_exposure: None. TAH operates exclusively in New Zealand; revenue, costs and capital structure are entirely NZD-denominated.
key_input_costs: GP and Nurse Practitioner remuneration (largest cost; practitioner costs rose 19.1% YoY in H1 FY27 to $6.108M)
Technology, digital enablement and cybersecurity (Digital Clinical Portal build-out; explicit management commitment to increased investment from H1 FY27)
Lease costs for GP clinic premises

recent_developments.event: TAH released unaudited H1 FY27 results (six months to 30 September 2026): group revenue $12.867M (+20.8% YoY), EBITDA $3.700M (+34.1% YoY), statutory NPAT $2.104M (+38.4% YoY, of which $1.841M attributable to shareholders, +30.2% YoY), diluted EPS 18.50 cents (+30.1% YoY). ARC Medical Services revenue grew to $9.153M from $6.840M (+33.9%) with segment profit before tax up 63.3% to $2.696M; Community GP revenue fell slightly to $3.714M from $3.813M (-2.6%) with segment profit before tax falling to $258k from $494k. The Chairman's letter announced formal decentralisation of ARC Medical Services (under new GM Crystal Murphy) and Community GP (under new GM Greg Clarke) into distinct operating businesses, and flagged a deliberate increase in cybersecurity/technology investment plus an active programme to simplify systems and processes accumulated through rapid growth.

In October 2026, TAH vacated the premises of the closed Belmont Medical Centre and derecognised the associated lease (liability down $185k, right-of-use asset down $162k, estimated gain of $23k) — the final step in exiting the practice closed earlier in 2026 following safety incidents.
Board declared a fully imputed Q2 FY27 interim dividend of 4.00 cents per share, consistent with the fixed quarterly dividend policy established in FY26.

TAH paid in full the $498,750 deferred contingent consideration owed on the September 2025 acquisitions of ARC Health Limited and Cicada Health Limited, closing out that open balance-sheet item with no disclosed dispute or clawback.

TAH released its Q1 FY27 (quarter to 30 June 2026) unaudited trading update: group revenue up 20.9% YoY to $6.082M, ARC-related revenue up 33.2% YoY to $4.223M, statutory NPAT up 33.1% YoY to $865k, NPATA up 36.3% YoY to $1.025M. ARC services extended to 124 facilities (+37.8% YoY). Organic (ex-acquisition) enrolled patients declined 2.0% YoY overall, with ARC organic enrolments up 2.5% YoY offset by a 6.7% YoY decline in Community GP organic enrolments.

Health Minister Simeon Brown announced that 86% of GP practices voted in favour of Health NZ's 2026-27 primary care funding package, confirming implementation of the demographically-reweighted capitation formula effective 1 July 2026 (6.32% base increase, guaranteed minimum 4% per-practice increase, $128.4M additional government investment). Cabinet separately agreed to review the capitation formula every five years, with the first review from 2028.

TAH released its audited FY26 Annual Report (year ended 31 March 2026): revenue $22.488M (+17.9% YoY), EBITDA $5.747M, statutory NPAT $3.091M (+24.7%), underlying NPATA $3.634M (+25.9%), diluted EPS 28.38 cents (+24.8%), full-year dividend 16.00 cps (+8.8% YoY). The Chairman's letter disclosed the forced closure of Belmont Medical Centre, confirmed no further Community GP acquisitions, and disclosed ARC GM Niomi Fleming's departure for health reasons at end of July 2026 (her eventual successor is now confirmed as Crystal Murphy, per the H1 FY27 report).

TAH issued a patient information update regarding the Manage My Health (MMH) cybersecurity breach that occurred in late 2025; no material financial impact was disclosed. Management's subsequent H1 FY27 commentary indicates heightened and sustained attention to cybersecurity as a result.

TAH acquired 80% of ARC Health Limited (Canterbury) and 70% of Cicada Health Limited (Bay of Plenty/Tauranga), effective 1 September 2025, both immediately EBITDA-accretive with founders remaining active co-owners. Both entities completed their first 12 months of Group ownership on 31 August 2026 and transitioned from 'acquired businesses' to 'existing operations' reporting from September 2026.

items.target: No explicit numerical FY27 target disclosed; the H1 FY27 Chairman's letter adopts a notably more positive tone than the FY26 letter's 'difficult environment' framing, stating simply 'we had a good first half,' while flagging that increased cybersecurity/technology investment will absorb some short-term earnings
items.vs_prior: tone improved materially versus the FY26 letter's cautious framing, consistent with H1 FY27 actuals (revenue +20.8%, EBITDA +34.1%, NPAT +38.4% YoY) outperforming that prior caution
items.notes: No formal numeric FY27 revenue or earnings guidance has been issued at either the FY26 result, the Q1 FY27 update, or the H1 FY27 result. The qualitative tone has shifted from 'difficult... no near-term relief' (FY26 letter) to 'we had a good first half' (H1 FY27 letter), though management also signals it will accept 'some cost to short-term earnings' from increased technology/cybersecurity investment in H2 FY27.

items.target: 4.00 cents per share per quarter (16 cps annualised), fully imputed
items.period: FY27 (Q2 FY27 interim dividend of 4.00 cps declared as a subsequent event to the H1 FY27 report)
items.vs_prior: maintained at the fixed quarterly rate established for FY26, unchanged through Q1 and Q2 FY27
items.notes: Policy is a fixed quarterly cents-per-share amount (since FY26) rather than a payout-ratio target, providing shareholders certainty while preserving reinvestment flexibility. FY26 total dividend was 16.00 cps (+8.8% YoY vs FY25's 14.71 cps); both Q1 and Q2 FY27 dividends have been held flat at 4.00 cps.

items.target: ~20% of the NZ ARC population medium-term (originally framed as a 5-year target from FY24)
items.notes: Estimated at ~17-18% as of FY26, with ARC facility count at 124 as of the last disclosed figure (Q1 FY27, July 2026) and no more recent facility count disclosed in the H1 FY27 report. ARC segment revenue and profit growth accelerated further in H1 FY27 (revenue +33.9%, PBT +63.3% YoY), consistent with continued share gains, though the organic vs. acquisition-driven split is not separately disclosed.

items.target: Continued bolt-on ARC acquisitions; explicit halt on further Community GP acquisitions; opportunistic evaluation of non-healthcare recurring-revenue businesses
items.vs_prior: maintained; no new acquisition announced since Sept 2025 (over 14 months), and the deferred consideration on the last two acquisitions (ARC Health, Cicada Health) was paid in full during H1 FY27, closing that item
items.notes: Management's H1 FY27 letter reframes near-term capital priorities around operational simplification, people development, and 'allocating capital prudently,' with no new acquisition commentary; this is a softer M&A tone than in the FY26 letter, though it may simply reflect no deal being ready to announce rather than a change in strategy.

guidance.management_commentary: H1 FY27 Chairman's letter (John Fernandes, Executive Chairman): 'We had a good first half. Revenue increased 20.8% to $12.9 million and statutory net profit increased 38.4% to $2.1 million compared to the prior comparable period... ARC Medical Services and Community GP now operate as distinct businesses, led by Crystal Murphy and Greg Clarke respectively... One thing we could have done better as we grew was to be more deliberate about keeping the businesses simple... We are now actively working to simplify this, consolidating systems and improving the information available to the people running each business. Last year we noted the availability of clinical talent as our primary operational risk. That remains important, although our focus on resilience has broadened to include cybersecurity and the technology infrastructure that increasingly underpins the delivery of healthcare. We expect to increase our investment in these areas, accepting some cost to short-term earnings in return for greater durability over time. Our priorities for the rest of the year are simple: delight our customers, develop our people, continuously improve the businesses we own, and allocate capital prudently.' This is a markedly more upbeat and self-critical/transparent tone than the FY26 letter, candidly naming both the growth success (ARC) and an internal operating weakness (accumulated complexity) that is being actively addressed.

bull_case: Structural demographic tailwind is among the most powerful and certain long-duration growth drivers available on the NZX: NZ's 65+ population share is projected to nearly double by 2073, and the 85+ cohort (highest ARC utilisation) grows fastest of all. TAH is the only NZX-listed pure-play services provider (not a property owner like Ryman or Summerset) positioned to capture this trend directly.

H1 FY27 results confirm genuine operating leverage in the ARC segment, not just revenue growth: ARC segment revenue +33.9% YoY but segment profit before tax +63.3% YoY and segment EBITDA +66% YoY, alongside the now-implemented, more generous capitation formula (6.32% base uplift plus reweighting) flowing through ARC capitation revenue, which grew 57% YoY in the half.

Momentum broadly accelerated rather than faded from FY26 into H1 FY27: group revenue growth of +20.8% YoY and NPAT growth of +38.4% YoY mark an improvement on the already-strong FY26 print (+17.9% revenue, +24.7% NPAT), with management's own tone shifting from 'difficult environment, no near-term relief' to 'we had a good first half.'

Deliberate decentralisation (dedicated GMs for ARC and Community GP from H1 FY27) and candid management acknowledgement of accumulated operational complexity, paired with an active simplification programme, suggest a management team disciplined enough to address its own weaknesses proactively rather than let them compound — a positive governance signal for a fast-growing roll-up.

High and resilient profitability with real operating leverage: underlying trends point to continued margin durability (H1 FY27 cost of services fell to 48.9% of revenue from 49.4% YoY despite clinician wage pressure), the business is asset-light and capital-light, and the fixed, growing quarterly dividend (16 cps annualised, held flat through Q1 and Q2 FY27) is well-covered by cash generation ($3.0M cash at 30 Sept 2026, modest ~$3.4M total debt).
bear_case: Community GP segment profitability is deteriorating faster than its revenue: segment profit before tax nearly halved YoY in H1 FY27 ($258k vs $494k) on only a 2.6% revenue decline, and the new dedicated GM (Greg Clarke) has not yet demonstrated a turnaround through a full reporting cycle — this remains an unresolved drag on ~29% of group revenue.

The clinical workforce shortage is structural and, by management's own repeated account, is the binding constraint on ARC growth, not demand; practitioner costs rose 19.1% YoY in H1 FY27, and any acceleration in wage inflation could outpace the benefit of the new capitation formula.

Leadership and structural transition risk is real and recent: both the ARC GM (Crystal Murphy) and Community GP GM (Greg Clarke) are new to their decentralised roles as of H1 FY27, following successive departures (Niomi Fleming, Lucy Wu's acting tenure), and management itself has flagged that rapid growth left the business more operationally complex than it should have been — execution of the new structure and the simplification programme is not yet proven over time.

No new M&A has been announced in over 14 months, and the H1 FY27 Chairman's letter's capital-allocation language has shifted toward internal simplification rather than acquisitions — if this reflects a genuinely thinner deal pipeline rather than mere caution, the growth algorithm investors have become accustomed to (bolt-on ARC acquisitions) may slow.

Micro-cap illiquidity persists with zero identified sell-side analyst coverage (TipRanks, Simply Wall St, Stockopedia all show 0 covering analysts) and a history of extreme price dispersion (the Chairman himself cited a ~3x FY26 trading range of NZ$2.50-$7.50 as unrealistic), making the stock difficult to value, size in a portfolio, or trade without material price impact.
